arXiv:1109.2113v2 [math.AC] 09 Dec 2011

A characterization of Keller maps

Piotr Jędrzejewicz Affiliation: Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science Affiliation: Nicolaus Copernicus University Affiliation: Toruń, Poland
Abstract

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero. Let φ\varphi be a kk-endomorphism of the polynomial algebra k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. It is known that φ\varphi is an automorphism if and only if it maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible polynomials. In this paper we show that φ\varphi satisfies the jacobian condition if and only if it maps irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials. Therefore, the Jacobian Conjecture is equivalent to the following statement: every kk-endomorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], mapping irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials, maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible polynomials.

1 Introduction

Throughout this article kk is a field of characteristic zero. By k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] we denote the kk-algebra of polynomials in nn variables. If φ\varphi is a kk-endomorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], then by Jac⁡φ\jac\varphi we denote the jacobian determinant of the polynomials φ⁡(x1)\varphi(x_{1}), …\dots, φ⁡(xn)\varphi(x_{n}) with respect to the variables x1x_{1}, …\dots, xnx_{n}. If Jac⁡φ∈k∖{0}\jac\varphi\in k\setminus\{0\}, then we say that φ\varphi satisfies the jacobian condition. In this case the respective polynomial map F:kn→knF\colon k^{n}\to k^{n}, F⁡(x1,…,xn)=(φ⁡(x1),…,φ⁡(xn))F(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=(\varphi(x_{1}),\dots,\varphi(x_{n})), is called a Keller map. The famous Jacobian Conjecture, stated by Keller in [11], asserts that every kk-endomorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] satisfying the jacobian condition is an automorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Van den Essen and Shpilrain asked in [5], Problem 1, if every ℂ\mathbb{C}-endomorphism of ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] mapping variables to variables is an automorphism (recall that by a variable we mean an element of any set of nn generators). The affirmative answer was given by Jelonek in [7], Theorem 2. It was noted that this fact holds for arbitrary algebraically closed field of characteristic zero ([3], a comment to Theorem 10.5.9 on p. 273). Another characterization of polynomial automorphisms was obtained by Bakalarski in [1], Theorem 3.7 (see also a remark at the end of [1]). He showed that a ℂ\mathbb{C}-endomorphism of ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] mapping irreducible polynomials to irreducible polynomials is an automorphism. We present another proof of Bakalarski’s theorem for an arbitrary field kk of characteristic zero (Theorem 5.2).

The aim of this paper is to obtain a characterization of polynomial endomorphisms satisfying the jacobian condition as those mapping irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials (Theorem 5.1). Hence, using the result of Bakalarski, we have the following equivalent formulation of the Jacobian Conjecture: every kk-endomorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] mapping irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible polynomials (Theorem 5.3). Our characterization of kk-endomorphisms satisfying the jacobian condition is an immediate consequence of Theorem 4.1, where we prove that an irreducible polynomial gg divides the jacobian of given polynomials f1f_{1}, …\dots, fnf_{n} if and only if there exists an irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] such that g2g^{2} divides w⁡(f1,…,fn)w(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}).

Basic definitions and facts are presented in Section 2. In Section 3 we prove preparatory lemmas, which will be useful in the proof of Theorem 4.1, given in Section 4. In Section 5 we obtain a characterization of endomorphisms satisfying the jacobian condition and the equivalent formulation of the Jacobian Conjecture. Some conclusions and comments are presented in Section 6.

2 Preliminaries

By a ring we mean a commutative ring with unity. Let AA be a ring. An additive map d:A→Ad\colon A\to A such that d⁡(a​b)=d⁡(a)​b+a​d​(b)d(ab)=d(a)b+ad(b) for a,b∈Aa,b\in A is called a derivation of AA. The set Ad={a∈A;d⁡(a)=0}A^{d}=\{a\in A;\;d(a)=0\} is called the ring of constants of dd. If KK is a subring of AA, then a derivation dd of AA is KK-linear if and only if K⊂AdK\subset A^{d}. In this case we call dd a KK-derivation. Hence, if AA is a kk-algebra, where kk is a field, and a1,…,am∈Aa_{1},\dots,a_{m}\in A, then a map d:A→Ad\colon A\to A is a k⁡[a1,…,am]k[a_{1},\dots,a_{m}]-derivation if and only if dd is a kk-derivation and d⁡(ai)=0d(a_{i})=0 for i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m.

If dd is a kk-derivation of a kk-algebra AA, where kk is a field, then for an element a∈Aa\in A and a polynomial w⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]w(x)\in k[x] we have d⁡(w⁡(a))=w′​(a)​d​(a)d(w(a))=w^{\prime}(a)d(a). More generally, for a1,…,am∈Aa_{1},\dots,a_{m}\in A and a polynomial w(x1,…,xm)∈k[x1,w(x_{1},\dots,x_{m})\in k[x_{1}, OPEN…,xm]\dots,x_{m}] the following holds:

d⁡(w⁡(a1,…,am))=∂w∂x1​(a1,…,am)​d​(a1)+…+∂w∂xm​(a1,…,am)​d​(am).d(w(a_{1},\dots,a_{m}))=\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{1}}(a_{1},\dots,a_{m})d(a_{1})+\ldots+\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{m}}(a_{1},\dots,a_{m})d(a_{m}).

In particular, if dd is a kk-derivation of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], then d⁡(f)=∂f∂x1​d​(x1)+…+∂f∂xn​d​(xn)d(f)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}d(x_{1})+\ldots+\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}d(x_{n}) for every polynomial f∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero, let AA be a finitely generated kk-domain (that is, a commutative kk-algebra with unity, without zero divisors) and let RR be a kk-subalgebra of AA. Denote by R0R_{0} the field of fractions of RR. Nowicki ([13], Theorem 5.4; [12], Theorem 4.1.4) proved that the following conditions are equivalent:

(1)(1) R=AdR=A^{d} for some kk-derivation dd of AA,

(2)(2) RR is integrally closed in AA and R0∩A=RR_{0}\cap A=R.

Daigle observed in ”Locally nilpotent derivations” (unpublished lecture notes, available on his website) that the condition (2)(2) means that RR is algebraically closed in AA as a subring. The present author noted in [9] that this characterization holds also for KK-derivations, where KK is a subring of AA. In this case we have the following corollary from [9], Theorem 3.1.

Corollary 2.1.

Let AA be a finitely generated KK-domain of characteristic zero, where KK is a subring of AA. An element b∈Ab\in A belongs to the ring of constants of every KK-derivation of AA if and only if bb is algebraic over the field K0K_{0}.

Given nn polynomials f1,…,fn∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], by Jac⁡(f1,…,fn)\jac(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) we denote the jacobian determinant of f1,…,fnf_{1},\dots,f_{n} with respect to x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n}. Note that the map d⁡(f)=Jac⁡(f1,…,fn−1,f)d(f)=\jac(f_{1},\dots,f_{n-1},f) for f∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is a kk-derivation of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], such that d⁡(fi)=0d(f_{i})=0 for i=1,…,n−1i=1,\dots,n-1. More generally, given mm polynomials f1,…,fm∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], where 1⩽m⩽n1\leqslant m\leqslant n, and given arbitrary j1,…,jm∈{1,…,n}j_{1},\dots,j_{m}\in\{1,\dots,n\}, by Jacj1,…,jmf1,…,fm\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}}_{j_{1},\dots,j_{m}} we denote the jacobian determinant of f1,…,fmf_{1},\dots,f_{m} with respect to xj1,…,xjmx_{j_{1}},\dots,x_{j_{m}}. The map d⁡(f)=Jacj1,…,jmf1,…,fi−1,f,fi+1,…,fmd(f)=\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{i-1},f,f_{i+1},\dots,f_{m}}_{j_{1},\dots,j_{m}} for f∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is also a kk-derivation of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], and we have d⁡(fj)=0d(f_{j})=0 for j≠ij\neq i.

Following [10], we introduce the notion of a differential gcd of polynomials:

dgcd⁡(f1,…,fm)=gcd⁡(Jacj1,…,jmf1,…,fm, 1⩽j1,…,jm⩽n)\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})=\gcd\left(\jac^{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}}_{j_{1},\dots,j_{m}};\;1\leqslant j_{1},\dots,j_{m}\leqslant n\right)

for f1,…,fm∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. Of course, dgcd\dgcd is defined with respect to a scalar multiple. For a single polynomial f∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] we have dgcd⁡(f)=c⋅gcd⁡(∂f∂x1,…,∂f∂xn)\dgcd(f)=c\cdot\gcd\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}},\dots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}\right), where c∈k∖{0}c\in k\setminus\{0\}. For nn polynomials f1,…,fn∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] we have dgcd⁡(f1,…,fn)=c⋅Jac⁡(f1,…,fn)\dgcd(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})=c\cdot\jac(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}), where c∈k∖{0}c\in k\setminus\{0\}.

Note the following easy observation.

Lemma 3.2.

Let m∈{1,…,n}m\in\{1,\dots,n\}.

a) The elements f1¯,…,fm¯∈A\overline{f_{1}},\dots,\overline{f_{m}}\in A are algebraically dependent over kk if and only if g|w⁡(f1,…,fm)g\mid w(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) for some nonzero polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}].

b) Let i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\dots,m\}. The element fi¯∈A\overline{f_{i}}\in A is algebraic over the field k⁡(f1¯,…,fi−1¯,fi+1¯,…,fn¯)k(\,\overline{f_{1}},\dots,\overline{f_{i-1}},\overline{f_{i+1}},\dots,\overline{f_{n}}\,) if and only if g|w⁡(f1,…,fm)g\mid w(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) for some nonzero polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}] of positive degree with respect to xix_{i}.

In the case of nn polynomials in nn variables we have the following.

Lemma 3.3.

There exists an irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] such that g|w⁡(f1,…,fn)g\mid w(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}).

Proof.

The ideal (g)(g) has height 11, so the Krull dimension of AA equals n−1n-1. Hence, the elements f1¯,…,fn¯\overline{f_{1}},\dots,\overline{f_{n}} are algebraically dependent over kk. Then, by Lemma 3.2.a, there exists a nonzero polynomial u∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]u\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] such that g|u⁡(f1,…,fn)g\mid u(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}). The polynomial uu is obviously non-constant. Then, for some irreducible factor ww of uu, the polynomial w⁡(f1,…,fn)w(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) is divisible by gg. ∎

Lemma 3.4.

Assume that n⩾2n\geqslant 2 and 0⩽r⩽n−20\leqslant r\leqslant n-2. Consider polynomials u1∈k⁡[x1,…,xr,xr+1]∖k⁡[x1,…,xr]u_{1}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{r},x_{r+1}]\setminus k[x_{1},\dots,x_{r}] and u2∈k⁡[x1,…,xr,xr+2]∖k⁡[x1,…,xr]u_{2}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{r},x_{r+2}]\setminus k[x_{1},\dots,x_{r}]. If the degrees of u1u_{1} with respect to xr+1x_{r+1} and of u2u_{2} with respect to xr+2x_{r+2} are relatively prime, then there exist nonzero polynomials w1∈k⁡[x1,…,xr]w_{1}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{r}], w2∈k⁡[x1,…,xr,xr+1,xr+2]∖k⁡[x1,…,xr]w_{2}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{r},x_{r+1},x_{r+2}]\setminus k[x_{1},\dots,x_{r}] such that w2w_{2} is irreducible and u1+u2=w1​w2u_{1}+u_{2}=w_{1}w_{2}.

Proof.

Consider a decomposition of u1+u2u_{1}+u_{2} into irreducible factors in k[x1,k[x_{1}, …,xr,xr+1,xr+2]\dots,x_{r},x_{r+1},x_{r+2}]: u1+u2=v1​…​vs​vs+1​…​vtu_{1}+u_{2}=v_{1}\ldots v_{s}v_{s+1}\ldots v_{t}, where v1,…,vs∈k[x1,…,v_{1},\dots,v_{s}\in k[x_{1},\dots, xr]x_{r}] and vs+1,…,vt∉k⁡[x1,…,xr]v_{s+1},\dots,v_{t}\not\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{r}], 0⩽s⩽t0\leqslant s\leqslant t. Observe that s<ts<t, because u1+u2∉k⁡[x1,…,xr]u_{1}+u_{2}\not\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{r}].

Now, consider the field L=k⁡(x1,…,xr)L=k(x_{1},\dots,x_{r}). Since the degrees of the polynomials: u1u_{1} in L⁡[xr+1]L[x_{r+1}] and u2u_{2} in L⁡[xr+2]L[x_{r+2}] are positive and relatively prime, the polynomial u1+u2u_{1}+u_{2} is irreducible in L⁡[xr+1,xr+2]L[x_{r+1},x_{r+2}], by Corollary 3 to Theorem 21 in [14], p. 94 (see also [2]). Hence t=s+1t=s+1. Finally, put w1=v1​…​vsw_{1}=v_{1}\ldots v_{s} (w1=1w_{1}=1 if s=0s=0) and w2=vs+1w_{2}=v_{s+1}. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

Let w∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}] be an irreducible polynomial such that ∂w∂xi≠0\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{i}}\neq 0 for some i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\dots,m\}. Then there exist polynomials v1,v2∈k⁡[x1,…,xm]v_{1},v_{2}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}] and v∈k⁡[x1,…,xi−1,xi+1,…,xm]∖{0}v\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\dots,x_{m}]\setminus\{0\} such that

v1​w+v2​∂w∂xi=v.\textstyle v_{1}w+v_{2}\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{i}}=v.
Proof.

Consider the field L=k⁡(x1,…,xi−1,xi+1,…,xm)L=k(x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\dots,x_{m}). The polynomial ww is irreducible in L⁡[xi]L[x_{i}], and the polynomial ∂w∂xi\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{i}} is nonzero, so they are relatively prime in L⁡[xi]L[x_{i}]. Hence there exist polynomials u1,u2∈L⁡[xi]u_{1},u_{2}\in L[x_{i}] such that

u1​w+u2​∂w∂xi=1.\textstyle u_{1}w+u_{2}\frac{\partial w}{\partial x_{i}}=1.

Let vv (v∈k⁡[x1,…,xi−1,xi+1,…,xm]v\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\dots,x_{m}]) be the least common denominator of the coefficients of polynomials u1u_{1}, u2u_{2}. Multiplying the above equality by vv and denoting v1=u1​vv_{1}=u_{1}v, v2=u2​vv_{2}=u_{2}v we get the lemma. ∎

4 Irreducible factors of jacobians

Note the following immediate consequence of Theorem 4.1.

Corollary 4.2.

For arbitrary polynomials f1,…,fn∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] the following conditions are equivalent:

(i)(i) Jac⁡(f1,…,fn)∈k∖{0}\jac(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\in k\setminus\{0\},

(i​i)(ii) for every irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] the polynomial w⁡(f1CLOSE,w(f_{1}, OPEN…,fn)\dots,f_{n}) is square-free.

5 An equivalent formulation of the Jacobian Conjecture

If φ\varphi is a kk-endomorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], then by Jac⁡φ\jac\varphi we denote the jacobian determinant of the polynomials φ⁡(x1)\varphi(x_{1}), …\dots, φ⁡(xn)\varphi(x_{n}) with respect to x1x_{1}, …\dots, xnx_{n}:

Jac⁡φ=Jac⁡(φ⁡(x1),…,φ⁡(xn)).\jac\varphi=\jac(\varphi(x_{1}),\dots,\varphi(x_{n})).

We obtain the following characterization of kk-endomorphisms satisfying the jacobian condition.

Theorem 5.1.

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero. Let φ\varphi be a kk-endomorphism of the polynomial algebra k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i)(i) Jac⁡φ∈k∖{0}\jac\varphi\in k\setminus\{0\},

(i​i)(ii) for every irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] the polynomial φ⁡(w)\varphi(w) is square-free.

Proof.

Put f1=φ⁡(x1)f_{1}=\varphi(x_{1}), …\dots, fn=φ⁡(xn)f_{n}=\varphi(x_{n}). Since φ\varphi is a kk-endomorphism, for every polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] we have

φ⁡(w⁡(x1,…,xn))=w⁡(φ⁡(x1),…,φ⁡(xn))=w⁡(f1,…,fn).\varphi(w(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))=w(\varphi(x_{1}),\dots,\varphi(x_{n}))=w(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}).

The rest follows from Corollary 4.2. ∎

The following theorem was obtained by Bakalarski in [1] (Theorem 3.7) under an additional assumption, but it was noted in a remark added in the proof that this assumption is not necessary. Here we present another proof of Bakalarski’s theorem, based on our Lemma 3.3.

Theorem 5.2 (Bakalarski).

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero and let φ\varphi be a kk-endomorphism of the polynomial algebra k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i)(i) φ\varphi is a kk-automorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}],

(i​i)(ii) for every irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] the polynomial φ⁡(w)\varphi(w) is irreducible.

Proof.

Every automorphism of a ring maps irreducible elements into irreducible elements, so it is enough to prove the implication (i​i)⇒(i)(ii)\Rightarrow(i). Assume that φ⁡(w)\varphi(w) is an irreducible polynomial for every irreducible w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. Observe that φ\varphi is a monomorphism: if φ⁡(f)=0\varphi(f)=0 and f=g1​…​grf=g_{1}\ldots g_{r} is a decomposition into irreducible factors, then φ⁡(gi)=0\varphi(g_{i})=0 for some ii, contrary to the assumption.

Now we will prove that φ\varphi is surjective. Put fi=φ⁡(xi)f_{i}=\varphi(x_{i}) for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. Suppose that there exists a polynomial g∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], such that g∉k⁡[f1,…,fn]g\not\in k[f_{1},\dots,f_{n}]. In this case at least one of irreducible factors of gg does not belong to k⁡[f1,…,fn]k[f_{1},\dots,f_{n}], so we may assume that gg is irreducible. Then, by Lemma 3.3, g|w⁡(f1,…,fn)g\mid w(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) for some irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], that is, w⁡(f1,…,fn)=g​hw(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})=gh, where h∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]h\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. However, h∉kh\not\in k, because g∉k⁡[f1,…,fn]g\not\in k[f_{1},\dots,f_{n}], so w⁡(f1,…,fn)w(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) is a reducible polynomial. ∎

By Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 we have.

Theorem 5.3.

Let kk be a field of characteristic zero, let nn be a positive integer. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i)(i) every kk-endomorphism φ\varphi of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] such that Jac⁡φ∈k∖{0}\jac\varphi\in k\setminus\{0\} is an automorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] (the Jacobian Conjecture),

(i​i)(ii) every kk-endomorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] mapping irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible polynomials.

6 Final remarks

Remark 1. From Theorem 5.1 we know that a kk-endomorphism φ\varphi of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] satisfies the jacobian condition if and only if it maps irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials. It is natural to ask if there exists a non-trivial example of such a kk-endomorphism; non-trivial in the following sense: for some irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] the polynomial φ⁡(w)\varphi(w) is reducible. From Theorem 5.3 we know that such an example would be a counter-example to the Jacobian Conjecture, and if such an example does not exist, the Jacobian Conjecture is true.

Remark 2. It may be interesting to consider the following property of a given ring (a commutative ring with unity):

every endomorphism mapping irreducible elements to square-freeelements maps irreducible elements to irreducible elements.\begin{array}[]{l}\mbox{every endomorphism mapping irreducible elements to square-free}\\ \mbox{elements maps irreducible elements to irreducible elements.}\end{array} (∗)
Question 6.1.

Let RR be a unique factorization domain satisfying the condition (∗)(\ast). Does the ring R⁡[x]R[x] of polynomials in one variable over RR also satisfy the condition (∗)(\ast)?

If the answer to this question is positive, then the Jacobian Conjecture is true. Namely, in this case, by an obvious induction, every ring endomorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] mapping irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible polynomials. And then, in particular, every kk-endomorphism of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] mapping irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible polynomials.

Remark 3. Theorem 4.1 is a multi-dimensional version of the following lemma of Freudenburg ([6]): if an irreducible polynomial g∈ℂ⁡[x,y]g\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] divides both partial derivatives ∂f∂x\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, ∂f∂y\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} of a given polynomial f∈ℂ⁡[x,y]f\in\mathbb{C}[x,y], then gg divides f+cf+c for some c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C}. Van den Essen, Nowicki and Tyc ([4]) generalized this lemma for nn variables over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 00. In [8] the author obtained the following generalization for an arbitrary field kk of characteristic 00 (not necessarily algebraically closed): an irreducible polynomial g∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] divides all partial derivatives ∂f∂x1\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}, …\dots, ∂f∂xn\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}} of a given polynomial f∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] if and only if g2g^{2} divides W⁡(f)W(f) for some irreducible polynomial W⁡(T)∈k⁡[T]W(T)\in k[T].

Let us take a closer look at a very specific analogy between the cases of a single polynomial and of nn polynomials. In fact, comparing the proofs, we may argue that there is no real analogy here. The only crucial implication for a single polynomial f∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is the following: if an irreducible polynomial g∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] divides ∂f∂x1\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}, …\dots, ∂f∂xn\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}, then gg divides W⁡(f)W(f) for some irreducible polynomial W⁡(T)∈k⁡[T]W(T)\in k[T]. For nn polynomials f1,…,fn∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{n}\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] and an irreducible polynomial g∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], without any assumptions, there always exists an irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] such that gg divides w⁡(f1,…,fn)w(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}). We have established this fact in Lemma 3.3.

Now, for a single polynomial f∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] it is easy to show that if an irreducible polynomial g∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] divides ∂f∂x1\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}, …\dots, ∂f∂xn\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}} and W⁡(f)W(f), where W⁡(T)∈k⁡[T]W(T)\in k[T] is an irreducible polynomial, then g2g^{2} divides W⁡(f)W(f). The analog of this fact for nn polynomials is, in general, not true, as the following example shows.

Example 6.2 (Gwoździewicz, Jelonek).

Consider the following polynomials in k⁡[x,y]k[x,y]: f1=xf_{1}=x, f2=x​yf_{2}=xy, g=xg=x and w=xw=x. Then Jac⁡(f1,f2)=x\jac(f_{1},f_{2})=x and w⁡(f1,f2)=xw(f_{1},f_{2})=x are divisible by gg, but w⁡(f1,f2)w(f_{1},f_{2}) is not divisible by g2g^{2}.

However, we still can prove that if gg divides the jacobian of f1f_{1}, …\dots, fnf_{n}, then there exists an irreducible polynomial w∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]w\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] such that g2g^{2} divides w⁡(f1,…,fn)w(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}). Finally, the reverse implication is also not easy to be proved, in contrast to the case of a single polynomial. It is an easy exercise to show for f,g∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]f,g\in k[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], where gg is irreducible, that if g2g^{2} divides W⁡(f)W(f) for some irreducible polynomial W⁡(T)∈k⁡[T]W(T)\in k[T], then gg divides ∂f∂xi\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}} for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n.
